title: Plain bread, hungry
hook: arriving late and tired, Seneca finds dry bread delicious (Letters 123)

segments.voice: Yesterday: night people, the Romans who lived backwards to be noticed. Your line was with the sun. Did you make it to bed at the hour you named? Day four hundred eighty-nine.

Everyone has had the best meal of their life, and an odd number of them were terrible. Gas station crackers after a long hike. Cold toast after a night in a hospital waiting room. Instant noodles at two in the morning after a move. Letter 123 opens with Seneca arriving at his country house in the Alban hills, late at night, worn out from a trip that was more uncomfortable than long. Nothing is ready. The cook isn't ready, the baker has no fresh bread, the house is dark. And Seneca, of all people, is about to discover something about plain bread. Today: plain bread, hungry.
screen: `THE BEST MEAL: GAS STATION CRACKERS.` → `LATE, TIRED, NOTHING READY.` → `SENECA AND THE DRY BREAD.`

segments.voice: First, nothing is ready, and that's fine. Seneca says he lies down to rest and lets the cook and the baker take their time. Nothing is heavy, he says, if you take it calmly; nothing is worth anger that you can simply wait out. A tired man in a dark house decides not to make it worse. Second, the bread. The baker has none, so someone finds some: the steward, the doorkeeper, a tenant. It's coarse and dry. Bad bread, Seneca imagines someone protesting. Wait, he answers, it'll get better. Hunger will make it soft. And it does. He eats it and finds it good. Third, hunger as the seasoning. The idea is older than Seneca. The Roman writer Cicero passes on a saying of Socrates: hunger is the best seasoning for food, and thirst for drink. Seneca adds his own rule to it: don't eat until your stomach asks. The body, he says, is a better judge of what's delicious than the cook. Fourth, what this is for. Not a plan to starve yourself, and not a lecture against good food. Seneca's point is freedom. Someone who can only be happy with fresh bread is hostage to every baker. Someone who's learned that plain bread tastes fine when you're truly hungry can arrive late, anywhere, and be content. The sauce, it turns out, was in him the whole time.
screen: `NOTHING READY, AND THAT'S FINE.` · `DRY BREAD: WAIT, HUNGER WILL SOFTEN IT.` · `SOCRATES: HUNGER IS THE BEST SEASONING.` · `FREE FROM EVERY BAKER.` · then, large: `HUNGER IS THE SAUCE.`

segments.voice: Check in with your body right now. Are you hungry, really? On a scale of one to ten. Notice whether you often eat before the number climbs, out of habit, boredom or the clock. Now picture your next meal as the simplest version of itself: bread, rice, fruit, something plain. Imagine waiting until your body actually asks, and then tasting the first bite with all of that hunger. If you have any health reason not to wait, simply notice the hunger without testing it. The bell holds the time.
Plain bread. Coarse, dry, found by a doorkeeper late at night, and delicious to a man who was truly hungry. Today's word.
Your line: hunger is the sauce. Once today, eat something plain, and only when you're actually hungry. Notice what it tastes like. Day four hundred eighty-nine.

howItsDone: Some people practicing Stoic simplicity occasionally eat plain food and wait for real hunger before meals, to learn that contentment doesn't depend on fine things.

original.note: Latin, 'hunger': in Cicero's version of Socrates' saying, the best seasoning for food.

trapdoor: what you thought: good food needs a good cook.
what it means: real hunger makes plain bread taste good, and that makes you free of every baker.
what a scholar hears: Cicero, On Ends 2.90, gives Socrates' line 'cibi condimentum esse famem'; Seneca's letter puts the old saying into a small scene from his own late life.
